Abstract
Latency prediction for stream processing tasks (SPTs) is a critical issue for stream computing, parameter tuning, load opti-
mization, task scheduling, etc. This study addresses the real-time, volatile, and high-volume nature of streaming workloads
to improve latency prediction accuracy. A novel model based on Auto-encoders and Transformers was proposed to address
the above challenges. The Auto-encoder is utilized to reduce the dimensionality of the extensive features and generate a
compressed feature representation. Subsequently, the Transformer is employed to extract spatio-temporal dependencies and
predict the latency of SPTs. Experimental results on six benchmarks (about 260,000 samples in total) demonstrate that com-
pared to state-of-the-art models, the proposed model achieves higher accuracy and lower error rates, with average errors of
0.11% (M AE), 0.02% (RMSE), respectively, and average accuracy of 0.89. Moreover, a time window length of 60 or 80
allows the model to achieve the best average accuracy. Additionally, the ablation study veriﬁed that the Transformer signif-
icantly improved the prediction performance. These results conﬁrm that the proposed model can accurately predict latency
for SPTs, further laying the foundation for intelligent and proactive optimization of stream processing systems (SPSs).
Keywords Streaming data · Stream processing task · Latency prediction · Transformer

2 Related work
Latency prediction for stream processing tasks (SPTs) uses
two main approaches: model-driven and data-driven. This
section provides a description of SPTs and discusses model-
driven and data-driven methods.
2.1 Stream processing task (SPT)
An SPT, executed in SPSs such as Apache Storm, Spark
Streaming, or Apache Flink, is represented as a directed
acyclic graph (DAG) consisting of sources, operators, and
sinks as vertices, and streams as edges. Each source con-
tinuously receives external streaming data, while each sink
continuously sends computed results from operators to exter-
nal storage. Operators transform one or more input streams
into new output streams. Figure 1 illustrates an exemplary
SPT.
InFig.1,thecomponentsincludestreamingdata,SPT,net-
work, and servers. The SPT continuously receives a diverse
range of streaming data generated by devices (e.g., mobil-
ity devices, smart furniture, autonomous vehicles, etc.) from
the message queue, such as Kafka (Wei et al. 2025), Rab-
bitMQ (Pacella et al. 2025), and Elasticsearch (Nolte et al.
2025), through a source in the DAG. It sends computed
results to external storage, such as distributed ﬁle systems
and data warehouses, through a sink in the DAG. Typi-
cally, an SPT comprises various types of operators. The
real-time latency of an SPT is inﬂuenced by multiple factors,
including the characteristics of the distributed environment
(e.g., memory, bandwidth usage, etc.), data (e.g., arrival
amount, arrival rate, etc.), and the task itself (e.g., opera-
tor type, number of upstream/downstream channels, etc.).
Consequently, accurately predicting the latency of an SPT
becomes challenging due to the complex dynamics exhibited
when running in an SPS. The ﬁgure demonstrates the dis-
tributed and multi-operator nature of SPTs, contextualizing
the challenges addressed by the proposed model, highlights
the complexity of SPTs, emphasizing the need for latency
prediction models to account for multi-operator dependen-
cies and dynamic resource usage.

2.2 Model-driven methods
Model-driven latency prediction relies on analytical mod-
els and explicit assumptions. They aim to understand the
inherent rules within the task, construct mathematical mod-
els, and solve them. For example, Repantis and Kalogeraki
(2008) proposes a hotspot-based model to estimate opera-
tor execution time and data rate, and Gulisano et al. (2017)
uses time- and record-window models to predict operator
latency and throughput. While these studies effectively pre-
dict the performance of individual operators, they fall short
in predicting the overall performance, such as the latency,
of a speciﬁc SPT due to the presence of multiple types of
operators. In Lohrmann et al. (2015), a coarse-grained pre-
diction model based on the parallelism degree of operators
in SPTs was proposed, but it could not accurately predict
the speciﬁc latency value of an SPT. Similarly, in De Mat-
teis and Mencagli (2016), a latency prediction model based
on average latency and calculation time was constructed, but
it was also unable to predict the latency value of a speciﬁc
task. Other approaches, such as those presented in Wei et al.
(2019) (models based on operators in pipeline technology),
Kalim et al. (2019) (models based on operators and tasks),
and Khare et al. (2019) (latency prediction models based
on linear chains of operators), have been proposed. These
methods are explainable “white-box" models but depend on
assumptions that often fail in real deployments, limiting their
practical accuracy.
2.3 Data-driven methods
Data-driven methods train regression or classiﬁcation mod-
els directly on historical execution data. These models aim
to uncover hidden rules within the data and generate pre-
diction and analysis results. For instance, in Gautam and
Basava (2019), the authors constructed a ridge regression-
based model that utilized conventional system features (e.g.,
CPU usage and memory usage) to predict the latency of
SPTs. However, this approach overlooked the dynamic fea-
tures of tasks in an SPS. In Cardellini et al. (2018), the
authors employed reinforcement learning (Milani et al. 2024)
to map the relationships between tasks and resources and
allocate resources accordingly. Additionally, a reinforcement
learning-based model was used to predict the performance
of operators and tasks. However, these studies did not specif-
ically predict the true performance values. Furthermore, in
Gontarska et al. (2021), the authors evaluated the precision of
performance prediction using different models, such as expo-
nential smoothing and differential integrated moving average
auto-regressions. Despite the valuable contributions made by
these studies in performance prediction for operators or tasks,
only a limited number of features were utilized. Notably, the
authors proposed a deep-gated recurrent unit network-based
model to predict the throughput of SPTs (Chu et al. 2020).
The model achieved accuracy rates of 0.91, 0.90, 0.91, and
0.93 on four open-source benchmarks, respectively. These
results demonstrate the effectiveness of deep learning-based

Compared to prior work, our contributions are:
1. We integrate task, environment, and data-arrival features
into a single multivariate time series.
2. We combine an auto-encoder with a Transformer to
compress high-dimensional inputs and model long-range
dependencies.
3. We predict a precise latency value rather than broad per-
formance metrics.
The research on stream processing based on Transformer
has achieved remarkable breakthroughs in dynamic resource
allocation and latency prediction. In Fragkoulis et al. (2024);
Cardellini et al. (2022), the authors analyzed the challenges
in latency prediction of SPTs. In Nekooei-Joghdani and
Saﬁ-Esfahani (2025), the authors proposed a streaming task
scheduling framework based on multi-head attention, which
can dynamically allocate computing resources according to
real-time data. However, it fails to solve the problem of
high-dimensional feature compression, resulting in a rela-
tively high model complexity. Compared with traditional
time series models such as LSTM, GRU, etc, Transformer
performs better in long-distance dependency modeling. In
addition, Transformer has numerous applications across var-
iousﬁelds,suchasindynamicmodelingofproteintranslation
(Shao et al. 2024), remote sensing and soil moisture predic-
tion (Kuang et al. 2025), and medical image analysis (Li et al.
2025; Guo et al. 2025), etc. Regarding the computational
complexity problem of the Transformer, recent optimiza-
tion directions include sparse attention mechanism (Peng
and Zhao 2024), linearized attention (Han et al. 2023), and
lightweight design (Zayed et al. 2024), etc. In terms of feature
compression, existing studies on Transformer do not explic-
itly handle high-dimensional features. Here, we perform
end-to-end dimensionality reduction with an auto-encoder
to ﬁlter redundant features. We then capture spatio-temporal
operator relationships via DAG encoding and self-attention.

in SPS. Conversely, data-driven methods offer the advantage
of easily obtaining insights into the future and generating
executable rules.

The proposed model aims to predict the latency of SPTs
using an Auto-encoder neural network and a Transformer
neural network. Figure 3 provides an overview of the pro-

3.3 Auto-encoder neural network
There are several methods available for reducing the dimen-
sions of the original features and extracting meaningful
features from massive features, including PCA (Lin et al.
2024), LDA, t-SNE (Skrodzki et al. 2024), etc. Moreover,
there are three main types of study used for feature selection,
i.e., ﬁlter methods, wrapper methods, and embedded meth-
ods. However, these methods face certain limitations, one
of which is that dimension reduction for original data and
feature selection for massive features cannot be executed
simultaneously. For example, feature extraction requires a
separate step, dimension reduction requires a separate step,
and then the two steps are connected to achieve the feature
extraction and dimension reduction effect. This increases
the complexity of the process and may also increase the
ﬁnal error. Therefore, an end-to-end Auto-encoder neural
network is used to solve this problem, as shown in Fig. 4.
Compared to PCA and LDA, the Auto-encoder’s end-to-end
training avoids error accumulation from separate dimension-
ality reduction and feature selection steps.
As shown in Fig. 4, the Auto-encoder neural network
consists of an encoder g(·) and a decoder f (·). The Auto-
encoder neural network consists of an encoder g(·) and a
decoder f (·). The encoder maps the original data distribu-
tion to a compressed feature representation. Conversely, the

3.4 Transformer
Several methods have been proposed to model multivariate
time series data, such as auto-regressive integrated mov-
ing averages (ARIMA) (Khan et al. 2025), and recurrent
neural networks (RNN) (Tang et al. 2025), among others.
However, ARIMA was not chosen due to its dependence
on only observed data without utilizing state features. On
the other hand, RNNs suffer from the problem of long-term
dependency vanishing. Therefore, the Transformer is utilized
to model the compressed feature representation (multivari-
ate time series data). The Transformer has two signiﬁcant
advantages: the ability to capture long dependencies while
predicting long sequences and better training efﬁciency on
GPUs using distributed training. Figure 5 shows the entire
Transformer neural network.
As shown in Fig. 5, our proposed Transformer-based
latency prediction model follows the original Transformer
architecture (Vaswani et al. 2017). The model comprises
seven main components, including an input layer, a positional
encoding layer, four encoder layers, and a linear mapping
layer. In stage 1, the input layer, i.e., a fully-connected net-
work, maps the compressed feature representation to a vector
essential for adapting multi-head attention mechanisms. In
stage 2, the positional encoding layer encodes sequential
information in the output of the input layer through sine or
cosine functions. Then, it combines the input vector and the
positional encoding vector by element-wise addition. In stage
3, the combined vector enters four encoder layers, where
each encoder layer consists of four sub-layers, including a
self-attention layer and a feed-forward layer, followed by

In stage 4, the ﬁnal output of the encoder layer feeds into

Transformer’s ability to handle long-term dependencies.
In the context of SPTs, spatial dependencies refer to the
topological relationships between operators (e.g., upstream/
downstream connections in the DAG) and resource inter-
actions across distributed servers (e.g., CPU, memory, and
network usage). To capture these dependencies, the Trans-
former leverages two key mechanisms:
1. Positional Encoding: While positional encoding primar-
ily encodes temporal order, we extend it to incorpo-
rate spatial information by assigning unique positional
indices to operators based on their topological order in
the DAG. For example, operators closer to the source in
the DAG receive lower indices, enabling the model to
infer their spatial relationships.
2. Self-Attention Mechanism: The self-attention layer
computes pairwise correlations between all input fea-
tures, including operator types, parallelism, and server
resource metrics. This allows the model to learn implicit
spatial dependencies, such as how resource contention on
a server affects downstream operators or how upstream
operator throughput inﬂuences latency in connected
nodes. For instance, high attention weights between a
CPU-intensive operator and its downstream operator may
indicate a critical spatial dependency affecting latency.

4 Evaluation
In this section, we describe the experimental setup, error
comparison, and accuracy comparison to evaluate the effec-
tiveness of our proposed model.
4.1 Experimental setup
The experimental setup was designed to accurately reﬂect the
effectiveness of our proposed model, following the conﬁgu-
ration used in Chu et al. (2020). For predicting the latency
of SPTs, we utilized cross-validation (k = 10) and the Mean
Squared Error (MSE) cost function during run-time. The
model was trained using the Adam optimizer with a gradi-
ent clip of 4, a learning rate of 0.002, a mini-batch size of
64, a dropout rate of 0.3, and 2000 iterations. These hyper-
parameters were determined through a grid search algorithm
with ranges (learning rate: [0.001-0.01], time window length:
[20-100]).
A JobManager (Master) coordinates the distributed exe-
cution, scheduling tasks, and coordinating recovery from
failures. Sixteen Workers (TaskManagers) execute parallel
dataﬂow tasks, buffer, and exchange streaming data. During
the experiment, TaskManagers continuously read streaming
data from the Kafka node and send the results of task exe-
cution back to the Kafka node. Concurrently, the prediction
node constructs features and predicts the latency of SPTs
in real-time. The conﬁguration details for the Kafka node,
JobManager nodes, TaskManager nodes, and the prediction
node, are summarized in Table 1.

• GP: Grep extracts matching strings from text ﬁles, counts

• CIB: CPU-intensive benchmark splits received stream-
ing data into words, aggregates word counts, and sends

4.1.2 Baselines
To comprehensively and thoroughly verify the proposed
model, we evaluated it using six benchmarks. Among these,
three benchmarks are open source, and three were specif-
ically designed by us to execute distinct tasks. Firstly, all
six benchmarks were run on Apache Flink, a popular SPS.
Secondly, our real-time prediction framework collects vari-

Several factors could explain these experimental results in
terms of error and accuracy. Firstly, Baseline-1 predicts the
latency of stream join, which is only one type of operator in
SPT, thus neglecting the complexity of an SPT that typically
consists of multiple operators. Consequently, the prediction
performance of the proposed model is superior to that of
Baseline-1. Secondly, compared to Baseline-2 and Baseline-
3, which use ridge regression and GRU networks to predict
SPT latency, The Transformer learns spatiotemporal features
and long-term dependencies from input data streams. For
example, the positional encoding layer in the Transformer
captures spatial information, while the self-attention mecha-
nism extracts deep temporal features from the input data.
To be more speciﬁc, compared with the deep-gated recur-
rent unit network (Baseline-3), the proposed model has the
following advantages: (1) Global dependency capturing abil-
ity: The Transformer can model the dependencies between
any positions in a series simultaneously through its attention
mechanism, and is particularly good at capturing long-range
temporal associations. In SPT, latency can be determined by
the states of multiple historical time points, and the attention
mechanism can quantify the importance of these associa-
tions through weight allocation. In contrast, the Baseline-3
relies on the gradual transmission of hidden states by the
gate control unit, and its memory capacity is limited by
the series length. As the number of time steps increases,
early information may be lost due to gradient vanishing or
explosion, resulting in weaker modeling ability for long-term
dependencies. (2) Model expression ability: The proposed
model can learn diverse feature representations from differ-
ent subspaces through the attention mechanism. In latency
prediction, different attentions can focus on different fea-
tures respectively. The Baseline-3, on the other hand, relies
on ﬁxed-dimensional hidden states, and its feature extraction
ability is relatively singular, making it difﬁcult to capture the
complex patterns in multi-dimensional heterogeneous data.
Therefore, the proposed model has stronger advantages com-
pared with Baseline-3.

6 Conclusion
The aim of the present research was to accurately predict the
latency of Stream Processing Tasks (SPTs). To achieve this,
we proposed a novel model based on an Auto-encoder and
Transformer neural networks. The Auto-encoder neural net-
work is employed to reduce the dimensionality of extensive
features and generate a compressed feature representation
in the form of multivariate time series. The Transformer
network is employed to extract spatio-temporal dependen-
cies and predict the latency of SPTs. Experimental results
obtained from six benchmarks validate the effectiveness of
the proposed model.
The main results and ﬁndings of this paper can be sum-
marized as follows:
1. The proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art models
in terms of higher accuracy rates and lower error rates
across the six benchmarks.
2. The proposed model achieves optimal average accuracy
rates when the length of the time windows is set to 60 or
80.
3. The Transformer component of the proposed model sig-
niﬁcantly enhances prediction performance.
Limitations and future research directions The proposed
model, combining an Auto-encoder and Transformer neural
networks, exhibits higher computational complexity com-
pared to baseline models, as evidenced by longer training
and inference times. This complexity may limit its practical
deployment in resource-constrained environments. While the
study acknowledges the trade-off between prediction accu-
racy and computational efﬁciency, further optimization of the
model architecture is needed to reduce complexity without
sacriﬁcing performance. Additionally, future research direc-
tionscanenhancetheinterpretabilityandexplainabilityofthe
proposed model to provide insights into the factors and pat-
terns inﬂuencing SPT latency predictions. This could involve
developing visualization tools, feature importance analysis,
or model explanation techniques to help users understand
the model’s decision-making process and build trust in its
predictions.

Abstract: Latency prediction for stream processing tasks (SPTs) is a critical issue for stream computing, parameter tuning, load opti- mization, task scheduling, etc. This study addresses the real-time, volatile, and high-volume nature of streaming workloads to improve latency prediction accuracy. A novel model based on Auto-encoders and Transformers was proposed to address the above challenges. The Auto-encoder is utilized to reduce the dimensionality of the extensive features and generate a compressed feature representation. Subsequently, the Transformer is employed to extract spatio-temporal dependencies and predict the latency of SPTs. Experimental results on six benchmarks (about 260,000 samples in total) demonstrate that com- pared to state-of-the-art models, the proposed model achieves higher accuracy and lower error rates, with average errors of 0.11% (M AE), 0.02% (RMSE), respectively, and average accuracy of 0.89. Moreover, a time window length of 60 or 80 allows the model to achieve the best average accuracy. Additionally, the ablation study veriﬁed that the Transformer signif- icantly improved the prediction performance. These results conﬁrm that the proposed model can accurately predict latency for SPTs, further laying the foundation for intelligent and proactive optimization of stream processing systems (SPSs).
